diagnosis.what_is_wrong: The trace does not establish a kernel-level cause for the reported longer coding task. Several event rates are unusually high in the opening second and then fall, but CPU use is modest and targeted wake-to-run delays are only 0.002–0.011 ms; the evidence is insufficient to call this saturation or another fault.
diagnosis.evidence: Compared the full 03:20:35.900–03:20:54.000 trace and process lifetimes as recorded by ctf_timespan/ctf_proclife, then reviewed the full-span one-second event buckets and per-process sched_stat_runtime from run_python. In the first second sched_switch was about 5,665/s, sched_wakeup 2,899/s, and block issues/completes about 349/350/s; these fell in the next two seconds to averages of 654/s, 328/s, and 0/s. Yet measured CPU totaled only 5.453 CPU-seconds across the trace, and the targeted JSCWarmUp/JITWorker wake-to-run samples were 0.002–0.011 ms. Workers also cautioned that the broader wake/switch pairing was sparse and not attributable. No evidence in the notes identifies a responsible process or demonstrates a resource bottleneck; the operator-reported delay therefore is neither confirmed nor explained by this trace.
diagnosis.window_evidence: The only clear boundary is the opening-second activity drop, around 03:20:36.900: multiple event series fall together after the trace begins with a burst. That establishes a rate transition, not an incident window—the recording has no preceding in-span period to show what led into it, and the scheduler-delay checks do not support CPU starvation. I therefore cannot justify labeling any interval as the incident.
